triage.name: Intraventricular hemorrhage of newborn
triage.reason: Premature infant with apnea, lethargy or a drop in hematocrit; diagnosed by cranial ultrasound, an important cause of neonatal neurologic deterioration.

age.peak: first 3 days of life in very preterm infants

demographics: Occurs almost exclusively in preterm infants, especially those born before 32 weeks' gestation
Risk rises steeply with lower birth weight and lower gestational age
Uncommon in term infants, in whom it is usually related to birth trauma, asphyxia or a bleeding disorder

risk_factors.text: Respiratory distress syndrome or need for mechanical ventilation
Perinatal asphyxia or low Apgar scores

chief_complaints.text: The baby stopped breathing and went limp
The baby is not acting like himself — sleepy and not feeding
The baby's blood count dropped and the nurse said the baby looked pale

hpi.onset: Usually within the first 72 hours of life, often in the first 24–48 hours; may be clinically silent and detected only on screening cranial ultrasound
hpi.duration: Acute event, with ongoing risk over the first week of life
hpi.progression: May be sudden and catastrophic with apnea, pallor and shock, or gradual with subtle changes in activity, tone and feeding; a fall in hematocrit without another source is a common clue
hpi.location: Intracranial — germinal matrix and lateral ventricles
hpi.quality: Non-specific neonatal deterioration; no pain behavior described
hpi.severity: Ranges from clinically silent to catastrophic with shock and seizures
hpi.timing: Often sudden; may be recurrent apneic episodes

associated_symptoms.text: Pale color or a fall in hematocrit
Abnormal eye movements or fixed pupils

pertinent_negatives: Maternal use of anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs

argues_against: Neonatal sepsis as the sole explanation
Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy as the only cause
Congenital heart disease as the primary cause
Necrotizing enterocolitis as the sole cause

atypical.how_it_differs: Term infants with IVH usually have a clear precipitant such as birth trauma, asphyxia or a coagulopathy, and may present with seizures rather than the apnea and pallor typical of preterm infants.
IVH in older children is rare and usually secondary to trauma, vascular malformation or a bleeding disorder; presentation includes headache, vomiting and focal deficits rather than neonatal apnea.

general.mild: Alert but with subtle changes in tone, activity or feeding; may look well between apneic spells
general.moderate: Lethargic and pale, with reduced spontaneous movement and poor feeding
general.severe: Ill-appearing, pale, hypotonic, with apnea and a tense fontanelle
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale or mottled, unresponsive, with apnea, seizures or shock

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin and mucous membranes in good lighting
Palpate the anterior fontanelle with the infant at rest and upright
Observe the infant's spontaneous activity and response to handling
findings.finding: Decreased level of consciousness or lethargy

findings.maneuver: Assess limb and truncal tone by passive movement and posture
Observe for abnormal repetitive movements and monitor for electrographic seizures
Inspect the eyes and test the pupillary light reflex
findings.finding: Abnormal eye movements or fixed pupils

findings.maneuver: Observe breathing and monitor for pauses in respiration
Auscultate the chest and observe work of breathing
findings.finding: Respiratory distress with retractions or grunting

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure and assess perfusion
Auscultate the heart and count the rate
Inspect the skin for petechiae and bruising

labs.caveat: A fall in hemoglobin without another bleeding source is a classic clue; a normal value does not exclude a small hemorrhage.
Follows the hemoglobin; a serial drop over hours is more informative than a single value.
Thrombocytopenia both predisposes to and worsens hemorrhage.
Prolonged in disseminated intravascular coagulation and in vitamin K deficiency of prematurity.
Low fibrinogen supports disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Hypoglycemia is a common and treatable cause of neonatal lethargy and apnea that must be corrected.
Hypocalcemia can cause seizures and jitteriness in preterm infants.
Hyponatremia may reflect syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone after an intracranial event.
Metabolic acidosis accompanies poor perfusion and shock.
Elevated with poor perfusion or shock.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line and screening study in preterm infants; can be done at the bedside without sedation or radiation

findings.text: Echogenic material in the germinal matrix or lateral ventricles
Periventricular hemorrhagic infarction (echodense parenchyma adjacent to the ventricle)
Normal study early on, with hemorrhage appearing on a later scan

imaging.preferred_when: When ultrasound is equivocal, when cerebellar or parenchymal injury is suspected, or for later prognostication

findings.text: Blood products in the germinal matrix, ventricles or parenchyma with signal depending on age of blood
Cerebellar hemorrhage not seen on ultrasound
Periventricular leukomalacia or white matter injury
Hyperdense blood in the ventricles or germinal matrix

imaging.preferred_when: When a hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus or congenital heart disease is suspected

findings.text: Patent ductus arteriosus with left-to-right shunting

initial.why: Baseline hemoglobin, hematocrit and platelets; a falling hematocrit supports hemorrhage
Detects coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation that worsens bleeding
Glucose, sodium, calcium and acid-base status in a deteriorating neonate
Assesses oxygenation, ventilation and metabolic acidosis in apnea or shock
First-line test to detect and grade intraventricular hemorrhage at the bedside

supporting.why: Clarifies equivocal ultrasound findings and detects cerebellar or white matter injury
supporting.only_if: ultrasound is equivocal or cerebellar injury is suspected

supporting.why: Looks for a patent ductus arteriosus or congenital heart disease contributing to instability
supporting.only_if: a hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus or structural heart disease is suspected

supporting.why: Marker of poor perfusion in shock
supporting.only_if: hypotension or poor perfusion is present

supporting.why: Rarely needed; may show bloody or xanthochromic fluid when meningitis is being considered
supporting.only_if: meningitis is suspected and the infant is stable enough for lumbar puncture

not_indicated.why: Exposes the neonate to radiation; ultrasound and MRI are preferred
Not routine; lumbar puncture is hazardous in an unstable infant with raised intracranial pressure
not_indicated.only_if: meningitis is suspected and the infant is stable enough for lumbar puncture

not_indicated.why: Not needed for the diagnosis of hemorrhage; consider only if sepsis is suspected
No role in the diagnosis of intraventricular hemorrhage

decision_points: Screen all infants born before about 32 weeks' gestation with cranial ultrasound in the first days of life
Repeat cranial ultrasound serially to detect progression and posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus
Treat hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia and shock immediately while arranging imaging
Avoid unnecessary handling, rapid fluid boluses and fluctuations in cerebral blood flow

criteria.name: Papile grading of intraventricular hemorrhage
criteria.summary: A four-grade ultrasound classification: grade I is hemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix; grade II is blood within the ventricles without ventricular dilatation; grade III is blood filling and dilating the ventricles; grade IV is periventricular hemorrhagic infarction (parenchymal involvement).
items: Grade I: germinal matrix hemorrhage only
Grade II: intraventricular blood without ventricular dilatation
Grade III: intraventricular blood with ventricular dilatation

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: A preterm infant with apnea, lethargy, poor feeding, temperature instability and shock can look identical to one with intraventricular hemorrhage.
differential.trigger: Any deteriorating neonate with apnea, lethargy or shock — treat for sepsis while imaging is arranged.

history: Risk factors for infection such as prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever or chorioamnionitis
Onset may be later than the first 72 hours in late-onset sepsis
No sudden drop in hematocrit without another source
exam: Fever or temperature instability prominent
Signs of a focus such as abdominal distension or skin lesions
Fontanelle usually flat rather than tense
labs: Leukocytosis or leukopenia with left shift
Thrombocytopenia may occur but coagulopathy is less typical
imaging: Cranial ultrasound shows no germinal matrix or intraventricular blood

differential.name: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
differential.why_considered: Perinatal asphyxia causes lethargy, seizures, hypotonia and apnea in a newborn and can coexist with intraventricular hemorrhage.
differential.trigger: Low Apgar scores, need for resuscitation at birth, or seizures in the first day of life.

history: Sentinel event such as placental abruption, cord prolapse or shoulder dystocia
Depressed Apgar scores and need for resuscitation at delivery
Encephalopathy evident from birth rather than a sudden deterioration after a stable interval
exam: Seizures, hypotonia and reduced reflexes from the first hours
Multiorgan involvement with renal or hepatic dysfunction
Fontanelle usually normal
labs: Severe metabolic acidosis on cord or early blood gas
imaging: MRI shows deep gray matter or watershed cortical injury rather than germinal matrix blood
Cranial ultrasound may be normal early

differential.name: Neonatal seizures from metabolic causes
differential.why_considered: Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia and hyponatremia cause lethargy, jitteriness, apnea and seizures that mimic a hemorrhage.
differential.trigger: Jitteriness, seizures or lethargy with a low bedside glucose in a preterm or growth-restricted infant.

history: Infant of a diabetic mother, small for gestational age, or poor feeding
Symptoms resolve with glucose or calcium correction
No sudden hematocrit drop
exam: Jitteriness that can be suppressed by gentle restraint
Normal fontanelle and no pallor
Tone and alertness improve after correction
labs: Low ionized calcium or total calcium
imaging: MRI may show no acute blood products

differential.name: Neonatal meningitis
differential.why_considered: Infection of the meninges causes lethargy, apnea, seizures, a bulging fontanelle and shock in a neonate.
differential.trigger: Fever, a bulging fontanelle or seizures with CSF pleocytosis.

history: Maternal infection or prolonged rupture of membranes
Progressive rather than sudden deterioration
Feeding intolerance and temperature instability
exam: Fever and toxic appearance
Bulging fontanelle with neck stiffness (often absent in neonates)
No pallor out of proportion to illness
labs: CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and low glucose
imaging: Cranial ultrasound may show echogenic meninges or ventriculitis but no germinal matrix hemorrhage

differential.name: Subdural hemorrhage from birth trauma
differential.why_considered: Traumatic delivery can cause intracranial bleeding with seizures, lethargy and a falling hematocrit.

history: Difficult delivery with forceps or vacuum extraction
Term or near-term infant rather than extreme preterm
Symptoms may appear in the first day after a traumatic birth
exam: Focal neurologic findings or asymmetric tone
Retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopy
Palpable cephalohematoma or skull fracture
imaging: Cranial ultrasound may miss subdural collections
CT or MRI shows extra-axial blood over the cerebral convexities or in the posterior fossa

differential.name: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
differential.why_considered: Venous thrombosis causes seizures, lethargy and hemorrhagic infarction in a neonate, especially with dehydration or a prothrombotic state.

history: Dehydration, sepsis or a central line
Family history of thrombosis
Progressive rather than sudden onset
exam: Seizures and focal deficits
Signs of dehydration or sepsis
Fontanelle may be full
labs: Thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy may be present
imaging: MRI with venography shows absent flow in a venous sinus
Hemorrhagic venous infarction in a non-arterial distribution

differential.name: Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (vitamin K deficiency bleeding)
differential.why_considered: Lack of vitamin K causes bleeding in the first weeks of life, including intracranial hemorrhage, with a falling hematocrit.

history: No vitamin K prophylaxis at birth
Breastfed infant without supplementation
Bleeding from the umbilicus, nose or gastrointestinal tract
exam: Bruising, petechiae or bleeding from puncture sites
Pallor and lethargy
No germinal matrix hemorrhage on imaging
labs: Prolonged PT and INR with normal platelet count and fibrinogen
Correction of coagulation after vitamin K administration
imaging: Intracranial hemorrhage may be present but is not confined to the germinal matrix
Cranial ultrasound shows blood in atypical locations

differential.name: Periventricular leukomalacia
differential.why_considered: Ischemic white matter injury in preterm infants causes later motor deficits and can be confused with hemorrhagic injury on early imaging.

history: Preterm birth with hypotension or hypocarbia
Often clinically silent early
No acute drop in hematocrit
exam: Later spastic diplegia and motor delay
No acute pallor or shock
imaging: Cranial ultrasound shows periventricular echogenicity or cystic change rather than blood
MRI shows white matter injury without germinal matrix hemorrhage

severity.mild: Grade I germinal matrix hemorrhage: often clinically silent, detected on screening cranial ultrasound; infant may have subtle changes in tone, activity or feeding.
severity.moderate: Grade II intraventricular hemorrhage without ventricular dilatation: apnea, lethargy, pallor and a falling hematocrit may be present; fontanelle may be full.
severity.severe: Grade III intraventricular hemorrhage with ventricular dilatation: marked lethargy, apnea, seizures, hypotonia and a tense fontanelle; risk of posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus.
severity.critical: Grade IV periventricular hemorrhagic infarction or massive hemorrhage with shock, seizures, fixed pupils and cardiovascular collapse; may be life-threatening.

red_flags.finding: Apnea or need for increased ventilatory support
red_flags.meaning: Acute neurologic deterioration; assess for hemorrhage and other causes

red_flags.finding: Sudden pallor with a falling hematocrit

red_flags.meaning: Raised intracranial pressure or posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus
Cortical irritation from blood or infarction; requires urgent evaluation and treatment
Shock from blood loss or associated sepsis; resuscitate immediately

red_flags.finding: Fixed pupils or abnormal eye movements
red_flags.meaning: Severe intracranial hypertension or brainstem involvement

complications.name: Posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus
clues: Ventricular dilatation on serial cranial ultrasound

complications.name: Periventricular hemorrhagic infarction
clues: Grade III or IV hemorrhage on ultrasound

special_populations.differences: Extremely preterm infants under 28 weeks' gestation are at highest risk and may have clinically silent hemorrhage detected only on screening ultrasound; serial imaging is essential.

Intraventricular hemorrhage in older children is rare and usually secondary to trauma, vascular malformation or a bleeding disorder; presentation includes headache, vomiting and focal deficits rather than neonatal apnea.

key_questions.question: How early was the baby born, and how much did the baby weigh at birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm birth before about 32 weeks' gestation and very low birth weight (under 1500 g) — the strongest risk factors for germinal matrix and intraventricular hemorrhage

key_questions.question: When did the baby's behavior change — how many hours or days after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset within the first 72 hours of life, often the first 24–48 hours; a sudden deterioration after a stable interval points to hemorrhage

key_questions.question: What exactly did you see — did the baby stop breathing, go limp, or turn pale?
key_questions.looking_for: Apnea, lethargy, hypotonia and pallor — the classic non-specific signs of neonatal neurologic deterioration

key_questions.question: Has the baby been feeding and tolerating feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding or feeding intolerance; a change from the baby's baseline

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any shaking, twitching, or staring spells?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures, which occur in a minority but indicate cortical irritation from blood or infarction

key_questions.question: Has the baby needed more breathing support, or had more apnea spells than before?
key_questions.looking_for: Escalating respiratory support or recurrent apnea — a red flag for acute neurologic deterioration

key_questions.question: Has the baby's blood count or color changed — did anyone mention a drop in the hematocrit or that the baby looked pale?
key_questions.looking_for: A falling hematocrit or pallor without another bleeding source, a classic clue to intracranial hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Did the baby receive vitamin K after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent vitamin K prophylaxis raises concern for vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a look-alike cause of intracranial hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Were there any problems around delivery — difficult delivery, forceps or vacuum, low Apgar scores, or need for resuscitation?
key_questions.looking_for: Birth trauma, perinatal asphyxia or need for resuscitation, which raise risk and suggest alternative or coexisting causes

key_questions.question: Did the mother have any infection, fever, or prolonged rupture of membranes before delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Risk factors for neonatal sepsis, which can mimic intraventricular hemorrhage and must be treated while imaging is arranged

key_questions.question: Does the baby have any known bleeding disorder, or is there a family history of bleeding problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Inherited coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia that would predispose to or worsen hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Is the baby on any medications, or did the mother take anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal or infant medications that increase bleeding risk

reasoning_points: Preterm infant, especially born before 32 weeks' gestation or under 1500 g, with a sudden change in neurologic status in the first 72 hours of life
Apnea, lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia and pallor — non-specific signs of neonatal deterioration
A falling hematocrit or new pallor without another bleeding source
Bulging or tense fontanelle, seizures, or abnormal eye movements suggesting raised intracranial pressure or cortical irritation
Cranial ultrasound showing echogenic blood in the germinal matrix or lateral ventricles, graded by the Papile classification
Sepsis, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy considered and addressed, since they mimic or coexist with hemorrhage
Coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia identified as a contributing or alternative cause of bleeding
Serial cranial ultrasound planned to detect progression and posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus

easy: Extremely preterm infant born before 28 weeks' gestation
Sudden apnea, pallor and lethargy in the first 24–48 hours of life
Falling hematocrit with no other bleeding source
Cranial ultrasound shows germinal matrix or intraventricular blood
medium: Clinically silent hemorrhage detected only on screening cranial ultrasound in a stable preterm infant
Preterm infant with apnea and feeding intolerance but no focal findings
Coexisting respiratory distress syndrome or patent ductus arteriosus distracting from the neurologic change
Term infant with seizures after a traumatic delivery
hard: Term infant with intraventricular hemorrhage from birth trauma, asphyxia or a bleeding disorder rather than prematurity
Infant with vitamin K deficiency bleeding presenting with intracranial hemorrhage and prolonged PT/INR
Deterioration attributed to sepsis or hypoglycemia when hemorrhage is also present
Grade IV periventricular hemorrhagic infarction with shock and fixed pupils
Early normal cranial ultrasound that later shows hemorrhage on repeat imaging
